title: Fault Tolerant Coresets
claim: A summary is built from data, then corrupted by an adversary, and a decoder must recover a valid summary.
layout: 4 boxes, left-to-right, labeled arrows between stages
description: A single horizontal row of four rounded rectangles joined by black arrows that read left to right. Each box is tinted a different pastel color. The first box is gray and holds P, labeled 'input dataset'. An arrow labeled 'construct' leads to a light blue box with Ω, 'ε-coreset' and |Ω| ≪ |P|. An arrow labeled 'corrupt' leads to a light orange box with Ω-tilde, 'corrupted coreset up to f adversarial changes'. An arrow labeled 'recover' leads to a light green box with Ω-star, 'recovered O(ε)-coreset'. Math symbols sit at the center of each box, and the verbs sit above the arrows. The eye starts at the gray P box and follows the arrows to the green result.
caption: Fault-tolerant coreset pipeline. From the input dataset $P$, we construct a coreset $\Omega$. An adversary then applies up to $\f$ corruptions, producing $\widetilde{\Omega}$. The goal is to recover from $\widetilde{\Omega}$ a set $\Omega^\star$ that is again a $O(\eps)$-coreset for the original dataset $P$.
abstract: Coresets are small weighted summaries of large datasets that help quickly evaluate some loss objectives on the input dataset. We mainly focus on coresets for the $k$-means objective, where the cost of the input dataset with respect to a set of $k$ centers is the sum of squared distances from each point to its closest center. A $k$-means $\varepsilon$-coreset $Î©$ satisfies $\mathrm{cost}(P,S)=(1\pm\varepsilon)\mathrm{cost}(Î©,S)$ for every set $S$ of $k$ centers, where $P$ denotes the input dataset. A long line of work has established near optimal $\varepsilon$-coreset size bounds for $k$-means. A key assumption in these works is that the coreset remains intact after construction. The question we ask is the following: if an adversary corrupts at most $f$ weighted entries of an $\varepsilon$-coreset, can we recover an $O(\varepsilon)$-coreset via a decoding algorithm that is given only the corrupted coreset. This models situations where entries of the coreset can be corrupted during storage or transmission, and recovery must proceed without access to the original dataset. Our main result shows that increasing the usual coreset size by an additive $O(fk/\varepsilon)$ yields a coreset that can be decoded into an $O(\varepsilon)$-coreset after any $f$ adversarial corruptions. This bound is achieved by sensitivity sampling, a widely used method for constructing coresets. Our result is optimal in the sense that any fault tolerant coreset, whose decoding algorithm only keeps a subset of the points must also have size $Î©(fk/\varepsilon)$. Our experiments demonstrate recovery under adversarial corruptions.
